\paragraph{Which verifier do the theorems describe (B.1)}\label{sec:gen-pubinput-B1}

The specification's, and only it. The three deployed verifiers (the Rust, the Python and the recursion guest all run the combined equation; \texttt{verify-{}gt-{}table-{}pub.\allowbreak{}md} section 7 established the same and it is confirmed above first hand) accept every transcript the Lean verifier accepts, and strictly more: the test at \texttt{b435631} (\texttt{t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}…\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}P\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}I\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}:\allowbreak{}1\allowbreak{}8\allowbreak{}4\allowbreak{}-{}\allowbreak{}2\allowbreak{}1\allowbreak{}0}) pins one transcript accepted by the words' equation and rejected per limb (\texttt{rStar}, \texttt{atStar}, \texttt{wordsEquation}). The blueprint (\texttt{:1053-{}1062}) says this and assigns the deployed check's knowledge soundness to Layer 12: \enquote{their knowledge soundness at \texttt{1/\allowbreak{}|E|} is a lemma of its own, and Layer 12 owes it.}

\textbf{Is Layer 12 the right place, and is \enquote{a lemma} the right shape? No, on both counts.}

\begin{itemize}
\item Layer 12's theorem is \texttt{verify\_\allowbreak{}iff\_\allowbreak{}compiled} (\texttt{:1218-{}1221}): the executable \texttt{verify} accepts exactly when the Fiat–Shamir compilation of the oracle verifier accepts. The oracle verifier is the composition of the phases, so its public-input step is \emph{this} verifier. If \texttt{verify} is written from the Rust (combined check, values sent pooled), the \enquote{iff} is false on the transcripts above. If \texttt{verify} is written per limb, \texttt{verify\_\allowbreak{}iff\_\allowbreak{}compiled} can hold, but then \texttt{verify} is not the deployed verifier, the differential fixture (an honest Rust proof, which passes both checks) cannot tell, and the deployed verifier's soundness is proved nowhere. In neither case is anything \enquote{owed by Layer 12} discharged by a lemma inside it.
\item The object that is owed is a \texttt{Phase.\allowbreak{}Security} of a different \texttt{Phase.\allowbreak{}Def}: the deployed verifier reads the same transcript but computes a different verdict and a different pool. Knowledge soundness is a property of the whole reduction against the seams; it is a phase-level object, and the place for it is Layer 8. Its statement, precisely:

\begin{leancode}
-- the deployed verifier: the words' equation, the values sent pooled
def deployedVerifier (I) : OracleVerifier []ₒ (I.Stmt × TableOut I) (TheOracle I) (I.Stmt × PubOut I) (TheOracle I) pSpec
    -- verify := do let cs ← queryValues; if checkWords I s r cs then pure (pooledFrom I s r cs) else failure
noncomputable def deployedPhase (I) : Phase.Def I (I.Stmt × TableOut I) (I.Stmt × PubOut I)   -- n = 2, err = 1/|E|
def deployedSecurity (I) : Phase.Security I (deployedPhase I) (Seam.table I) (Seam.pub I)
\end{leancode}

with \texttt{checkWords} as in C.5 (the words' equation when exactly two lines are sent, the per-value check otherwise, so that the verifier is total over instances and is the Rust's on leanISA's) and \texttt{pooledFrom} as in C.6. Its completeness is the argument of C.6 and C.5; its knowledge soundness at \texttt{1/\allowbreak{}|E|} rests on the algebraic lemma proved in C.13 (\texttt{accepts\_\allowbreak{}two\_\allowbreak{}challenges}) plus list plumbing.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{The alternatives.}

\begin{itemize}
\item (i) \emph{Model the deployed check in the phase and prove it.} Feasible and cheap: the key lemma is proved (eleven lines), the phase's other proofs carry over, the estimated total is about 120 lines. Its error is the same \texttt{1/\allowbreak{}|E|}, by the same degree-one argument in \texttt{E} instead of \texttt{K}. It makes the check load-bearing again (C.6: without the check, no \texttt{Phase.\allowbreak{}Security}), and it makes \texttt{verify\_\allowbreak{}iff\_\allowbreak{}compiled} provable for a \texttt{verify} written from the Rust.
\item (ii) \emph{Keep the specification's check and report upstream.} The specification and the three implementations disagree; the per-limb check is strictly stronger and costs one more field equation; the two are equally sound (the lemma) but not equally strict. This is a leanVM finding in its own right (an ambiguity of the specification rather than a bug: nothing is unsound), to be reported whichever way leanerVM goes. But keeping only the specification's verifier leaves the deployed one unproved and the refinement theorem unstateable.
\item (iii) \emph{Both.} Two \texttt{Phase.\allowbreak{}Def}s over the same schedule, both with \texttt{Phase.\allowbreak{}Security}, and a lemma that the specification's verifier's acceptance implies the deployed one's (the two equations per limb imply the equation on the words; on the values sent, so trivial). The master theorems are instantiated with the deployed phase; the specification's stays as the documented reference of §8.2.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Recommendation: (iii), with the deployed phase as the one the master theorems and Layer 12 consume, and the divergence reported to leanVM as an ambiguity of §8.2.} Reason: the report's object is deployment on L1; the theorem that matters is about the verifier that runs; the specification's verifier is one lemma away and documents intent. If only one is kept, keep the deployed one.

\paragraph{The honest prover's values (B.2)}\label{sec:gen-pubinput-B2}

The Lean prover sends \texttt{expectedValues I input r} (\texttt{:219}), the lines' values \texttt{(\allowbreak{}1 + r)·cell0 + r·cell1} computed from the statement. The Rust prover does the same: \texttt{i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}k\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{}F\allowbreak{}6\allowbreak{}4\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}[\allowbreak{}0\allowbreak{}]\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}0\allowbreak{})\allowbreak{},\allowbreak{} F\allowbreak{}6\allowbreak{}4\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}[\allowbreak{}1\allowbreak{}]\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}0\allowbreak{})\allowbreak{},\allowbreak{} r\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{})} with \texttt{i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}k\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{},\allowbreak{} h\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{},\allowbreak{} t\allowbreak{})\allowbreak{} =\allowbreak{} l\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{} +\allowbreak{} t\allowbreak{}·\allowbreak{}(\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{} +\allowbreak{} h\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{})} (\texttt{cpu/\allowbreak{}mod.\allowbreak{}rs:611-{}613}; \texttt{multilinear.\allowbreak{}rs:46-{}48}), where \texttt{l.\allowbreak{}pi} is the public input the layout was built from (\texttt{layout.\allowbreak{}rs:83}, \texttt{:471} \texttt{p\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{} =\allowbreak{} [\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}x\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}[\allowbreak{}0\allowbreak{}]\allowbreak{},\allowbreak{} e\allowbreak{}x\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}[\allowbreak{}1\allowbreak{}]\allowbreak{}]}). Neither evaluates the committed column. \textbf{They agree.} The blueprint says so (\texttt{:1039-{}1041}).

Does it matter? Not for the theorems: on the accepting path the value is the same as the column's extension (on an honest stack; the phase's docstring \texttt{:40-{}41}). It matters for what the message \emph{is}: a function of public data on both sides, hence redundant for the verifier, hence (C.4) checkable by any check or by none without loss of soundness in the oracle model. The one place it is not redundant is the Fiat–Shamir transcript, where it is absorbed (\texttt{ps.\allowbreak{}add\_\allowbreak{}scalar}, \texttt{:616-{}618}) and so binds later challenges, though to a value the verifier could derive. The test file's adversary model, \enquote{a prover that sends its true evaluation} (\texttt{trueValues}, \texttt{:45-{}47}), is the right one for the deployed design (values sent pooled) and is what the refutations of C.6 and C.7 use.

\paragraph{The flag \texttt{PublicLine.sent} (E)}\label{sec:gen-pubinput-E}

At \texttt{b435631}, \texttt{Spine/\allowbreak{}Instance.\allowbreak{}lean:100-{}114}:

\begin{leancode}
/-- A column whose first two cells the public statement fixes (§8.2: the two public words are
the first two memory cells). -/
structure PublicLine (S : Shape) where
  /-- The column. -/
  col : S.ColumnId
  /-- The value cell 0 must hold. -/
  cell0 : K
  /-- The value cell 1 must hold. -/
  cell1 : K
  /-- Whether the proof carries the value claimed for this column on the line through its two
  cells (§8.2: it does for the two low limbs of the memory, and not for the top limb, whose
  value is known to be zero). It fixes the transcript, not the relation. -/
  sent : Bool
  /-- The column has a cell 1. -/
  pos : 0 < S.τ col.1
\end{leancode}

\textbf{What the theorems say of it.} Nothing: \texttt{M3Holds} reads \texttt{col,\allowbreak{} cell0,\allowbreak{} cell1,\allowbreak{} pos} only (\texttt{PublicLinesHold}, D.1), and \texttt{publicInputSecurity I} holds for every \texttt{I}, so for every assignment of \texttt{sent}. Probe C.8 shows the other direction of the same fact: an instance with \texttt{sent = false} on its only line is served, and a verifier that drops unsent claims is refuted on it. So \texttt{sent} is bound by no theorem; what pins leanISA's choice \texttt{(\allowbreak{}true,\allowbreak{} true,\allowbreak{} false)} is (a) the blueprint's prose (\texttt{:834-{}836}, \texttt{:1037-{}1039}) and the status' decision 15, (b) the definition \texttt{leanIsaInstance.\allowbreak{}publicLines} when Layer 3 lands, and (c) Layer 12's differential fixture, the only thing that would reject a transcript with three or one scalars. Until (b) and (c) exist, the pin is prose.

\textbf{Does it enlarge what an auditor must trust?} By one Boolean per line, whose only effect in the phase as built is on the \emph{transcript's format} (which values are sent and checked): the pool does not depend on it beyond which claims carry a sent value, and with \texttt{pooled} reading the statement, not even that. In the deployed design (values sent pooled) \texttt{sent} decides which pooled values are prover-chosen, so it enters the soundness argument (the unsent lines' claims are at verifier-computed values, and their falsity is a bad challenge on its own). Either way the auditor's obligation is the same: \enquote{leanISA's instance sends exactly the two low limbs}, a transcript fact checked against the Rust (\texttt{:616-{}618}, \texttt{:747-{}749}).

\textbf{Does the specification need the notion?} Not as a notion: §8.2 is written for leanISA's three limbs and says \enquote{the prover sends \texttt{c\_\allowbreak{}0,\allowbreak{} c\_\allowbreak{}1}} and \enquote{with 0 for the top limb}. A phase over an abstract instance must say which lines have a scalar; \texttt{sent : Bool} is the least it can say.

\textbf{Simpler designs considered.}

\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Every line's value sent, the third line modelled \enquote{as in the specification}.} The specification's third claim has a constant value and no scalar; sending a scalar for it makes the transcript one scalar longer than leanVM's, so this is not the specification's protocol. Rejected.
\item \emph{A separate list of constant claims} (\texttt{publicLines} for the lines with a scalar, and a list \enquote{columns whose line is zero} for the rest). Same information, two fields instead of a flag; it hard-codes the constant \texttt{0}, which is leanISA's accident (cells \texttt{(\allowbreak{}0,\allowbreak{} 0)}), not a rule of the protocol. The flag is simpler and more general. Rejected.
\item \emph{Provenance in the claim's type} (a \texttt{ColumnClaim} that records whether its value came from the prover). This is the deployed design's need, and it is met more simply by pooling the values sent (\texttt{pooledFrom}) while the claim type stays as it is.
\item \emph{Deriving \texttt{sent} from the cells} (send a scalar unless the line's value is identically zero). A coincidence of leanISA's data, not a rule; would silently change the transcript for another instance. Rejected.
\end{itemize}

Verdict: the flag is the right primitive. Its cost is not the flag but the absence of anything that pins it (finding in G).

\paragraph{Statement checks (F)}\label{sec:gen-pubinput-F}

Each declaration read at \texttt{b435631} against what it should say. The library objects were introduced in C.0.

\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{verifier\_\allowbreak{}verify} (\texttt{:253-{}256}): as an ordinary verifier, on the transcript \texttt{tr}, the verdict is \texttt{pure (\allowbreak{}pooled I s (\allowbreak{}tr 0),\allowbreak{} o)} if \texttt{check I s (\allowbreak{}tr 0) (\allowbreak{}tr 1)} and \texttt{failure} otherwise. Reads the challenge at index 0 and the message at index 1 of the transcript, keeps the oracle \texttt{o}. Correct, and it is what the two proofs start from through \texttt{guarded} (\texttt{:273-{}276}).
\item \texttt{complete} (\texttt{:300-{}302}): \texttt{p\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}C\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{} i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{} i\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{} (\allowbreak{}S\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{} I\allowbreak{})\allowbreak{} (\allowbreak{}S\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{} I\allowbreak{})} for every initial state and implementation of the (empty) shared oracle. Direction right (input seam to output seam), no hypothesis beyond the seam, probability one (\texttt{perfectCompleteness} is completeness with error \texttt{0}, ArkLib \texttt{Security/\allowbreak{}Basic.\allowbreak{}lean:103-{}105}).
\item \texttt{rbr} (\texttt{:350-{}353}): \texttt{r\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}K\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}w\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}S\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}W\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}C\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}W\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{} i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{} i\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{} (\allowbreak{}S\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{} I\allowbreak{})\allowbreak{} (\allowbreak{}S\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{} I\allowbreak{})\allowbreak{} (\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{} \_\allowbreak{} ↦\allowbreak{} U\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{})\allowbreak{} (\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}x\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{} I\allowbreak{})\allowbreak{} (\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}F\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{} I\allowbreak{} i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{} i\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{})\allowbreak{} (\allowbreak{}f\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{} \_\allowbreak{} ↦\allowbreak{} e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{})}. The error function assigns \texttt{error} to every challenge index; there is one (index 0, \texttt{pSpec.\allowbreak{}dir 0 = .\allowbreak{}V\_\allowbreak{}to\_\allowbreak{}P}), so \texttt{1/\allowbreak{}|E|} is charged to \texttt{r} and nothing to the message round (a message round has no error in this definition). Right challenge.
\item \emph{Tightness.} The bound is attained: on the toy at statement \texttt{1} with \texttt{badLine} (column 2 = \texttt{[1,\allowbreak{} 1]}, outside the table seam), the pooled claim holds at \texttt{r = 0} and fails at the sampled \texttt{y} (\texttt{t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}…\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}P\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}I\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}:\allowbreak{}1\allowbreak{}1\allowbreak{}6\allowbreak{}-{}\allowbreak{}1\allowbreak{}1\allowbreak{}8}: (\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{} t\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{} s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}1\allowbreak{} 0\allowbreak{})\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}2\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{},\allowbreak{} c\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}H\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{} b\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}L\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}e} and \texttt{\#\allowbreak{}g\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{} ¬\allowbreak{} ∀\allowbreak{} c\allowbreak{} ∈\allowbreak{} (\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{} t\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{} s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}1\allowbreak{} y\allowbreak{})\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}2\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{},\allowbreak{} c\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}H\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{} b\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}L\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}e}). With at most one bad challenge (\texttt{bad\_\allowbreak{}challenge\_\allowbreak{}unique}) and one exhibited, the bad event has probability exactly \texttt{1/\allowbreak{}|E|} for that stack: the error cannot be lowered. A wrong statement gives the bad challenge \texttt{r = 1} (\texttt{:120-{}123}).
\item \texttt{stateFunction} (\texttt{:327-{}346}): round 0 the table seam; round 1 the public seam of the pool at the challenge; round 2 that and the check. \texttt{toFun\_\allowbreak{}empty} is \texttt{Iff.\allowbreak{}rfl} (round 0 is the input relation by definition), \texttt{toFun\_\allowbreak{}next} drops the check, \texttt{toFun\_\allowbreak{}full} is the guarded verdict lemma. The invariant after the challenge does not mention the message, which is why any message can be accepted (C.3).
\item \texttt{extractor} (\texttt{:317-{}321}): \texttt{extractMid}, \texttt{extractOut} return \texttt{(\allowbreak{})}. The witness types are \texttt{Unit} at every round: the stack is the oracle, and the extraction of the stack is the commit phase's (\texttt{Spine/\allowbreak{}Compose.\allowbreak{}lean:58-{}59}). Correct for this phase; the composition (\texttt{piopExtractor}) is what carries knowledge.
\item \texttt{publicInputPhase} (\texttt{:376-{}381}): \texttt{n := 2}, \texttt{pSpec}, the reduction, \texttt{err := fun \_\allowbreak{} ↦ error}. \texttt{noncomputable} for the real number only. \texttt{publicInputComplete} (\texttt{:384-{}388}), \texttt{publicInputSecurity} (\texttt{:391-{}397}): the two bundles the spine consumes; both quantify over \texttt{init impl} inside (the fields \texttt{complete}, \texttt{kSF}, \texttt{rbr} of \texttt{Component.\allowbreak{}Complete}/\texttt{Security}).
\item \texttt{\#print axioms}: not run on the originals after 09:18 (C.9). Run on the verbatim copy \texttt{Probe0Baseline.\allowbreak{}lean} (its \texttt{diff} against the source is the two namespace lines): \texttt{publicInputSecurity} and \texttt{publicInputComplete} depend on \texttt{[\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}p\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}x\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{},\allowbreak{} C\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}h\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{},\allowbreak{} Q\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}]}, no \texttt{sorryAx}: no admitted ArkLib theorem is in the closure. The earlier review reported the same for the reviewed names.
\item \emph{\texttt{pooled} takes the lines' values, not the values sent.} In the oracle verifier the pool is computed only on the accepting path, where \texttt{cs = expectedValues}, so the two agree there (\texttt{pooledFrom\_\allowbreak{}expected}, C.6, proved). Off that path the verifier rejects and pools nothing. For a future executable verifier that reads \texttt{pooled} and \texttt{check}, they agree as long as it runs \emph{this} check. They differ exactly on the transcripts of B.1 (the words' equation passes, the per-limb check fails): a \texttt{verify} written from the Rust pools the values sent there and accepts, this verifier rejects. So there is a path on which they differ, and it is the set of transcripts on which the two verifiers disagree.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Acceptance tests 7, 13, 14, 15 (F.2)}\label{sec:gen-layer1-F2}

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{7} (\texttt{:1284-{}1286}): \enquote{Lifting table \texttt{j} by \texttt{∏\_\allowbreak{}\{k ≥ τ\_\allowbreak{}j\} X\_\allowbreak{}k} sums to the table's own sum (\texttt{sumCube\_\allowbreak{}prodVars}) … Witness: \texttt{tableSummand\_\allowbreak{}target} on heights 2 and 1.} The statement it describes is \texttt{sumCube\_\allowbreak{}padHigh}, not \texttt{sumCube\_\allowbreak{}prodVars} (which is \texttt{Σ x\_\allowbreak{}0⋯x\_\allowbreak{}\{m−1\} = 1}); and \texttt{tableSummand\_\allowbreak{}target} does not exist (Layer 7 is not built). The existing witness is \texttt{tests/\allowbreak{}…/\allowbreak{}Padding.\allowbreak{}lean:44-{}49} (the copied table sums to 0 in characteristic two).
\item \textbf{13} (\texttt{:1303-{}1305}): the named witness exists (\texttt{t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}…\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}F\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}x\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}C\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}:\allowbreak{}3\allowbreak{}7\allowbreak{}-{}\allowbreak{}4\allowbreak{}7}) and fails on the reversed order. Met.
\item \textbf{14} (\texttt{:1306-{}1307}): \enquote{Witness: \texttt{bytecodeColumn\_\allowbreak{}slot} on a two-instruction program.} The theorem exists but restates the definition and holds of the opposite layout by the same proof (C.3); the witness that pins slot 3 = \texttt{(\allowbreak{}1,\allowbreak{}1,\allowbreak{}0,\allowbreak{}0)} is \texttt{b\allowbreak{}y\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}C\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}w\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}r\allowbreak{}\_\allowbreak{}b\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}V\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}c} and the oracle \texttt{\#guard}s at \texttt{t\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}t\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}…\allowbreak{}/\allowbreak{}F\allowbreak{}i\allowbreak{}x\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}d\allowbreak{}C\allowbreak{}o\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}u\allowbreak{}m\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}s\allowbreak{}.\allowbreak{}l\allowbreak{}e\allowbreak{}a\allowbreak{}n\allowbreak{}:\allowbreak{}8\allowbreak{}2\allowbreak{}-{}\allowbreak{}9\allowbreak{}3}. Stale.
\item \textbf{15} (\texttt{:1308-{}1310}): \enquote{Blocks sit at offsets that are multiples of their size, largest first; \texttt{stack\_\allowbreak{}eval} fails for any other placement. Witness: three blocks of sizes 4, 2, 1 with the small one first.} Two imprecisions: 4, 2, 1 are the \emph{heights} (the sizes, in the code's sense of variables, are 2, 1, 0); and \enquote{fails for any other placement} is false: sizes 1, 1, 2 in that order sit at offsets 0, 2, 4, all aligned (\texttt{DuplicatesProbe}), and any permutation of equal sizes is aligned too, which is exactly why the tie order needs its own guard (B.2). The witness exists (\texttt{tests/\allowbreak{}…/\allowbreak{}Stack.\allowbreak{}lean:87-{}95}).
\end{itemize}
